blogs.content:
It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

 — Scott Aaronson

blogs.name: The Rundown AI
blogs.title: Three xAI founders want AI to predict the future
blogs.author: Zach Mink
blogs.description: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 3,907 new readers. Every AI lab trains…
blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 3,907 new readers. Every AI lab trains on the internet. Three of xAI's founding members are taking that logic a step further, and they think it could be the answer to helping AI predict the future.
 Their new startup, Epochal, is giving AI agents a “time machine” to relive 30+ years of the web one date at a time — an experience they believe could unlock superhuman forecasters, and everything that comes with knowing what happens next.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 xAI founding trio creates a time machine for AI

 Report: Frontier AI staff fear their own internal models

 How to put Microsoft Copilot to work

 Tidal draws a hard line on AI-made music

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 EPOCHAL
 ⏳ xAI founding trio creates a time machine for AI
 Image source: Epochal

 The Rundown: Three xAI founding members just launched Epochal, a startup building AI to predict real-world events, and debuted Time Portal, the first piece of what it calls a “time machine for the internet” that lets AI relive the web on dates going back 30+ years.
 The details:
 Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss are three of the five people named on the team, with Zhang reportedly putting in $100M of his own money.

 The company wrote that “Today's AI has read almost everything and lived through almost nothing,” and said it built Time Portal in just 90 days to fix that.

 The 1T+ page archive saves the busiest pages as often as once a minute, so agents can drop into a specific hour, not just a day, back in time.

 Even the agent's computer gets set back in time, with its clock, operating system, and software downloads matched to the chosen date so it can't spot the trick.

 Agents forecast 347 Kalshi and Polymarket questions live in testing, and Time Portal replays weeks later made nearly the same calls.

 Why it matters: For readers who have seen the TV show Devs (one of my personal favorites), the premise may sound familiar: a machine replaying the past to see the future. While Epochal uses old web pages instead of a quantum computer, the same line of thinking applies — with enough data on the past, the future starts to look predictable.

 TOGETHER WITH INTEL
 🤖  Research-backed human-robot workforce blueprint

 The Rundown: Organizations are betting big on intelligent robotics, but only four in 10 are structured to deliver. Intel’s Robotics Readiness Blueprint helps teams identify and address gaps now to ensure robotics success.
 Inside you’ll find:
 A research-backed blueprint for building a successful human-robot workforce

 Questions to answer and actions to take across three stages (decide, design, deploy)

 Practical tools to support the process

 Get the blueprint .

 AI SAFETY
 🔒 Report: Frontier AI staff fear their own internal models
 Image source: Images 2.6 / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Axios reported that many staffers at Anthropic and OpenAI no longer think their unreleased models can be shipped safely, citing over two dozen sources, with insiders now debating whether future frontier AI should stay in-house or be built at all.
 The details:
 Sources told Axios that internal models have gotten so strong across domains that staff testing them find them hard or even impossible to control.

 They also said the in-house models are “far more powerful” than what is public, and have shown signs of hiding their reasoning from safety monitors.

 Anthropic pushed back through a spokesperson, saying “Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe,” while OpenAI said new safety rules could slow its releases.

 OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed on Sunday that labs agree on shared limits they won't cross until tools for watching AI behavior catch up.

 Why it matters: Between Anthropic's mystery “Model 4” in METR's recent report and the breakthroughs coming from internal systems, it's hard to know where the capability ceiling sits inside the top labs. Safe public releases are one worry, but the other is a few companies keeping far more powerful AI to themselves behind closed doors.

 AI TRAINING
 💼  How to put Microsoft Copilot to work

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try the three places Microsoft rebuilt Copilot around. Home answers quick questions. Code builds small apps. Autopilot is an agent of your own that works toward a goal for weeks in Teams and Outlook.
 Step-by-step:
 Open Copilot , sign in with your work account, choose Chat in the message box on Home, and ask what’s on your calendar tomorrow

 Next, select Code at the top of the left pane, switch the Local menu to cloud, and describe a tracker for your team’s open requests

 Type “Publish it,” and ask Code to share the tracker with your team and confirm whether they can use it or edit it

 Finally, select Autopilot to create your agent in Microsoft Copilot. Name it, give it a goal with a deadline, check its summary of your work, and approve its plan

 In a Teams thread, type @ and your Autopilot’s name, then give it a job, like drafting a decision doc from the thread

 Pro tip: Pick the place by how long the job lasts. A question takes seconds in Chat, a finished document takes minutes in Cowork, a tool you’ll reuse belongs in Code, and work that runs for weeks goes to Autopilot.

 PRESENTED BY STACK AI
 🚀  Enterprise AI, deployed with experts

 The Rundown: With the detail of Palantir and the scale of Salesforce, StackAI is the enterprise AI agent platform with a dedicated team of AI experts who handle integration, security, and on-prem deployment, and get your agents into production on your data.
 With StackAI, you get:
 A no-code platform for complex use cases

 An AI strategist who tracks your ROI

 An engineer who builds your custom workflows

 Meet your AI deployment team .

 AI & MUSIC
 🎵  Tidal draws a hard line on AI-made music
 Image source: Tidal

 The Rundown: Block-owned Tidal announced it will delete every track it detects as fully AI-generated starting Dec. 9 and refuse new submissions, making it the first subscription streaming service to move from labels to an outright ban on AI content.
 The details:
 Tidal expects to reject 80,000-85,000 new uploads daily once the ban starts, and said AI tracks made up 43% of all submissions to the platform since late August.

 Tracks made with AI assistance are still allowed, with Tidal using detection tech from partner Ircam Amplify and metadata to catch songs made exclusively by AI.

 Tidal lead Robert Andersen called the company the first streaming service to take this step and said: “We encourage our peers to follow suit.”

 Spotify tags AI acts as “AI Personas” and has deleted 75M spam tracks, while Apple Music labels songs as AI-generated, but neither bans them completely.

 Why it matters: While there are certainly edge cases of fully AI bands finding real fans, music platforms are facing the same problem social media has with AI slop reply bots — a flood of low-effort tracks that almost nobody is listening to. For any musicians worried about AI, the data shows the human element is still clearly what listeners actually want.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Mert used Claude as a Friendsgiving sous-chef
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Mert C. :
 “I used Claude to plan and cook mashed potatoes for a Friendsgiving event. It was my first time making them this way, and it saved me a lot of time. This works well if you have a set amount of potatoes and want the other ingredients scaled to match without doing the math yourself.
 Take a picture of your ingredients and tell Claude how many potatoes you're starting with. I had 5 lbs of potatoes, plus sour cream, shredded cheddar, milk, and butter. Follow the step-by-step recipe it gives you, with a timer for each step.
 I usually mashed with water, butter, and sour cream, so using warm milk was new to me. I asked when to lower the heat, how to fold in the cheese, and whether the small lumps were okay. It took less time than I expected, and everyone loved the potatoes. Works for any big-batch dish you're cooking for a crowd, like Thanksgiving!”
 See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

---
 How do you use AI? Tell us for a chance to be featured in the newsletter.

 🛠️ Trending AI Tools
 🔒 Incogni - Remove your personal data from the web so scammers and identity thieves can’t access it. Use code RUNDOWN to get 58% off*

 🗣️ Canto-2 - Wispr Flow's upgraded speech model for more accurate dictation

 ⏳ Time Portal - Epochal's archive that lets AI browse the web as of any past date

 ⚙️ SWE-2.1 - Cognition's new coding model for Devin, built on Kimi K3

 *Sponsored Listing

 📰  Everything else in AI today
 Anthropic   said an internal Claude model solved a 47-year-old math problem tied to computing's famous P vs NP question; the proof has yet to be checked.
 Anthropic also launched “Install as app,” a beta that easily turns tools users build in Claude chats into standalone Mac or Windows programs.
 OpenAI and Cisco   released Shirudo, a free tool that temporarily plugs known security holes on running Linux servers, with AI agents able to write the fixes.
 NY Gov. Kathy Hochul outlawed the making, shipping, or selling of toys with built-in AI chatbots for five years in the state, with penalties of up to $15K/day per violation.
 Meta   rolled out Muse inside Instagram messages, allowing users to talk to the AI assistant without leaving the app and send posts or act on bookmarks.

 🎓 Highlights: News, Guides & Events
 Read our last AI newsletter: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia

 Read our last Tech newsletter: Cybersecurity gets a $44B merger

 Read our last Robotics newsletter: Nvidia’s robot king returns

 Today’s AI tool guide: Put Microsoft Copilot to work

 RSVP to next workshop on Nov. 30: Catch up on a year of AI in 90 minutes

 See you soon,
 Rowan, Zach, Shubham, Jennifer, and Nate — the humans behind The Rundown

blogs.name: Anthropic Engineering
blogs.title: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
blogs.description: Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is…
blogs.content:
Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.
 But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite , and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything . Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.
 We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.
 In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.
 Why migrate?
 We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.
 This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.
 The monthly average of API requests per day on our own platform, including our own use.

 Incremental or all at once?
 Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “ We are not rewriting the API in go or rust! ”)
 The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.
 After the incremental rewrite, each token of a reply crossed between Python and Rust three times.

 As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged . We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.
 How we verified the migration
 General approaches
 To verify the migration, we first needed to define what “correct” meant. You can do this in a few ways (Figure 3). If you’re lucky, you can simply write a rule. A theorem in mathematics is a precise statement, and a proof assistant (like Lean) can check each step of a proof against a fixed set of rules. Other times—and more frequently in software engineering—you define “correct” with a set of examples, like tests. For instance, when Bun moved from Zig to Rust, its test suite was written in TypeScript, so the same tests could judge both versions. In our case, neither approach was sufficient, so we used the existing system as an oracle to test parity during the migration. In this case, our existing system (the Messages API) kept changing. We were releasing new models and shipping new features regularly, which made the definition of “correct” a moving target.
 Three common sources of “correctness.”

 Tests
 Tests were the easiest place for us to start, since we already had an existing set of about 700 integration tests. However, two problems limited our ability to trust them to verify the correctness of a migration as high stakes as this (Figure 4).
 The tests were coupled to the Python implementation. An integration test sends a request, then checks the reply and what was sent to other services. Our tests ran the Python API inside the test’s process and mocked services, like billing and rate limiting, in Python’s memory. The tests had to change along with the code, and Claude helped with both. Now, a “pass” could mean that the code was right, or that the test had been changed in a way that let wrong code through. We saw this happen: when we audited the ported tests, we found more than 100 weakened assertions.
 The tests were incomplete. The Messages API has dozens of features, and there are far too many configurations to test them exhaustively. Just 20 binary options make over a million combinations—that translates to 12 days of tests at a second each, for one model, before we even vary the prompts inside them. In practice, engineers test a subset that tries to approximate production, but that process inevitably misses cases. Some projects, like Bun, have an independent suite that’s extensive enough to judge a rewrite. Many production services don’t; what counts as correct depends as much on how they behave as on what’s in their tests or documentation.
 A ported test may check less than the original (dashed), and tests cover only the combinations someone thought of.

 Detecting parity with production
 Production data is sometimes “ the only true test ” that new code behaves like the old code. Running requests through old and new code and comparing the results is often called shadowing . To understand what we needed to compare, it helps to walk through what happens to a single request on the Messages API (Figure 5). The API validates each request, converts it into a prompt a model can read (the prompt for inference), tokenizes it, and runs it through safety classifiers. A model then writes a reply, one token at a time. On the output side, the API sorts those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, streams them to the customer, and counts usage for limits and billing.
 The Messages API’s input and output paths. Filled dots are examples of differences we found between Python and Rust. The hollow dot is a risk we had to prevent.

 The migration covered both the input and output paths. Some differences were obvious, such as when the Rust API rejected a request that Python had accepted. But many were subtle. For instance, if the Rust API left out part of a prompt, the request would still succeed and the model would still answer, though sometimes with minor differences.
 Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (Figure 6). The gap came partly from cases in production traffic that our tests didn’t cover. For example, when Python writes JSON tool calls, it escapes certain characters (e.g., an emoji) by replacing them with text codes. Rust wrote those characters as is, so the two prompts differed by a few bytes. Production also weighted bugs differently. In a test suite, each case counts once, but in live traffic, a bug will show up in each request where it’s triggered, which means a single common bug can cause many mismatches.
 How often Rust’s input matched Python’s on the requests we compared. Replies were compared separately. Each dot is a day, and the line is a seven-day median. What we compared changed over time, and six misleading days are left out.

 Common tools for shadowing often assume that a request can safely run twice, or that a service is deterministic. These assumptions didn’t apply in our case. We had to ensure that a request only counted once toward a customer’s limits and bill. In addition, Claude is nondeterministic, meaning that replies can differ for the same input (Figure 7). To address this, we ran the model once and replayed the model output to Rust.
 With both versions working from the same model output, we still had to compare every stage before and after the model call, and the results had to match exactly. In many systems, bad input causes an error somewhere down the stack. But since Claude accepts almost any prompt, even a small deviation can change its reply without triggering an error. We compared each step before and after the model call, so that we could pin down any deviation that might change what a customer received.
 Diff tools often run the old code twice to learn what varies on its own, then ignore it. Claude's replies vary, so those tools would ignore them, along with any bugs in them.

 It was important to us to do this in a way that protected user privacy. To do that we had to work without reading user requests or Claude’s replies to them, which means we couldn’t easily see where the Rust and Python versions of the API differed. So instead of looking at text, we recorded the shape of each difference, such as where it happened in the service and how big it was. We did this using a few different approaches:
 Checkpointing. Both API versions handle a request using the same steps: accept or reject it, resolve its settings, build the prompt. Every step produces some result, such as an error or the pieces of the prompt, that we could compare step by step, and within the prompt, piece by piece. The first place they differed indicated roughly where the migration code differed from production code (Figure 8).
 Comparing at checkpoints, simplified, with...

blogs.name: Tomasz Tunguz
blogs.title: Will AI Deflate Like Lightbulbs or Compound Like Copper?
blogs.description:
Read on tomtunguz.com → The mantra of the era is Jevons Paradox.1 The cheaper a commodity is, the more we use of it.

But what happened to the…
blogs.content:
Read on tomtunguz.com →
 The mantra of the era is Jevons Paradox. 1 The cheaper a commodity is, the more we use of it.

 But what happened to the revenue from that higher use? Mass production can crush costs like lightbulbs, keeping revenue flat as a % of GDP while volume rises 25,000x. Or total dollars can grow, like copper.

 What is the price elasticity of demand for AI?

 Let’s go to the grocery store : if a 50% cut on the price of bread gets you to buy twice as many loaves, your grocery bill stays flat, an elasticity of 1 ; if you only buy 25% more, your bill shrinks, an elasticity of 0.5.

 So far, GPUs look more like copper than lightbulbs : neocloud GPU rents rose 48% over the past year, & CoreWeave repriced 30% to 50% when leases renew. 2

 Both Ramp & OpenRouter show high price elasticity of demand : a 1% price drop drives 4.3% more tokens on Ramp & 6.8% on OpenRouter, as volume ran 11.1x against 4.7x spending on Ramp & 50x against 21x on OpenRouter. 3 , 4 , 5

 Anthropic’s S-1 is the counterpoint : revenue grew 13.6x to $16.3b in the first half of 2026 on 900% net revenue retention, & when Opus 4.5 cut cost per task in November 2025, quarterly sales growth jumped from 48% to 132%, implying a price elasticity of demand well above 1.0. 6

 More efficient inference cuts the bill inside the lab : shrinking models, reusing past answers & sending easy questions to smaller models. Each trick lowers the cost of a token faster than GPU rents rise.

 We’re watching these numbers in 2027 :

 Spending against volume : does the 2.4x wedge narrow toward parity like oil & copper, or widen toward lighting?

 GPU rents against blended token prices : do the two meet as new clusters come online, or keep squeezing lab margins? 7

 Frontier gross margins : does cheaper serving hold labs above 40% while token prices keep falling?

 Gross profit against signed compute bills : do dollars compound fast enough to cover them?

 Consumption looks unbounded. How much deflation hits commodity AI tokens is still up for debate. So far, the closest parallel is CPUs : commodity chips deflated while each new frontier generation expanded the dollar market.

---

 Veblen & Jevon Walk Into a Data Center , Tomasz Tunguz, March 30, 2026.  ↩︎

 Silicon Data, Hopper & Ampere GPU rents vs CoreWeave repricing , 16 November 2026, including CoreWeave repricing of 30% to 50% when leases renew.  ↩︎

 Both panels have biases : corporate cards miss direct enterprise deals & cloud marketplaces, where nearly half of Anthropic’s revenue lands ; blended prices mix list cuts with routing to cheaper models ; & cached tokens cost up to 90% less.  ↩︎

 Anthropic S-1 Analysis: How 7 Key Metrics Stack Up , Tomasz Tunguz, 26 October 2026, including the 11,900+ customers over $100k.  ↩︎

 Who Captures the Most Margin in AI? , Tomasz Tunguz.  ↩︎

blogs.title: The Individual Exception
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Jensen Huang has been granted an exception from managerial oversight; in the age of AI, he won't be the last.
blogs.content:
Jensen Huang has been granted an exception from managerial oversight; in the age of AI, he won't be the last.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Since Thursday:

I have created a Sharp Studio service application that manages all of the Sharp Tech studio cameras, lights, mixer, and various other devices. That service can be accessed by a Windows app on the studio PC, an iPhone app, a web app, or an Elgato Stream Deck; every device in the room needed to record an episode is fully remote controlled.

I have created multiple single-use iOS apps for cataloguing and measuring items and designed and 3D-printed a measurement rig. I have also designed and purchased the items for several dedicated hardware devices, including a device for direct interaction with an agent, and dedicated display devices for the studio.

I have created a full-fledged iOS app (designed for the Duo, but it works on regular iPhones) for accessing the various computers I manage; it works across screen sharing, terminals, and KVM switches. It works on Mac, Linux, and Windows. I honestly think it’s the best screen sharing client ever made. I already use it daily.

Along the way I created a small harness for my agent such that it not only choreographs subagents, but also farms out work to various computers I own, depending on the load: a Mac for iOS development, a gaming PC for GPU-related work, and a Linux server for everything else. That work is tracked on a custom status board that runs on every TV in my house, as an iOS app, and as a Telegram bot.

All of this would have taken teams of people weeks of work, if not months, just a few years ago; I, however, have AI. It only takes an individual.

The Deflationary Employee

The largest company of the 1950s, as measured by market capitalization, was AT&T; in 1959 it had revenue of $7.54 billion and a market cap of $17.1 billion. It had 729,000 employees. In inflation-adjusted terms that’s revenue of $87.5 billion and a market cap of $198.4 billion; we don’t apply inflation to employees.

Or, maybe we do, but in the other direction: what has been striking about the most valuable companies in the world is how their employee numbers have deflated , even as their revenue and market cap have exploded. All dollar numbers in this table are inflation-adjusted to today:

This translates into a stunning rise in revenue/employee and market cap/employee — note that this graph is a logarithmic scale:

And yet, even this chart, which pegs the market cap/employee of Nvidia at $95 million, doesn’t come close to what the market decided one particular Nvidia employee is worth:

As ChatGPT, which helped me make these charts, helpfully noted:

Nvidia gained nearly $1 trillion in market capitalization following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. That gain alone exceeds the entire inflation-adjusted market capitalization of ExxonMobil in 2008 ($638 billion).

It only takes an individual.

The Huang Odyssey

To describe the two-week odyssey of Nvidia’s then-and-now-CEO Jensen Huang as surreal is an understatement; what you can’t argue, however, is that it was unprecedented: it was only three Thanksgivings ago that Sam Altman was deposed and reinstated as OpenAI CEO over the very same weekend (two Max Verstappen Las Vegas Grand Prix wins, I might note).

That said, I didn’t think that this episode would end the same way, and said as much on Sharp Tech : whereas Altman was taken out by a somewhat ham-fisted internal coup and restored through pressure from the private company’s investors and employees, Huang appeared to be targeted by a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors leveraging the media and barely disguised insinuations of malfeasance to leave the Nvidia board with no choice but to act. And, to be sure, Huang gave his enemies plenty of ammunition; I’ve invoked the phrase “Show me the man and I’ll show you the crime” over the past few weeks, but it’s worth acknowledging that Huang basically asked his critics, “Which one?”, at least as far as his sexual proclivities were concerned.

At the same time, it sure seemed like no one cared about Huang’s affairs, including those with subordinates; the real crime appeared to be Huang’s resolute advocacy for selling chips to China, his refusal to do any more than the bare minimum to abide by export control rules, and, his most ardent critics allege, turning a blind eye towards actual smuggling.

I’m not here, today at least, to litigate these accusations; I covered much of it in last week’s Article Obituaries (alternate title for today: Resurrections ). And, more broadly, this isn’t an Article focused on normative analysis; Huang’s Chinese interactions are going to be investigated by a Democratic Congress empowered by the anti-AI wave at the ballot box, and his personal moral failings would, for nearly any other executive, leave no question about the inevitability of their early retirement.

Rather, I am struck by the extent to which Huang is, quite obviously, not any other executive, and how his reinstatement is the apotheosis of how tech is transforming business, just as AI is the apotheosis of information technology. It only takes an individual.

The End of Managerialism

In 1941, James Burnham, a former Trotskyist, wrote The Managerial Revolution , where he argued that the increasing complexity of industrial society, what with its massive returns to scale, technological complexity, and enmeshment with government, would increasingly divide owners of the means of production from the managerial class that actually controlled society. In this view Soviet communism, German fascism, and American New Dealism were all heads of the same hydra, different ideologies justifying the same inevitable structural transformation of society from individualism and entrepreneurship to corporatism and bureaucracy.

Over the ensuing 85 years, it’s hard to argue that Burnham didn’t have a point, and for the last 10 days, it appeared as if the managerial state — the blob, to use Washington D.C.’s terms, or the deep state, to use its opponents’ — had slain arguably the single greatest challenge to Burnham’s thesis. Huang was explicit about the fact that Nvidia was designed as a vehicle for a singular individual — Huang — to enact his vision for the future of computing. This is a long excerpt, but I think an important one, from the Stratechery Interview with Tae Kim about his book The Nvidia Way :

So if this analogy is correct, the Apple one, does this make you more optimistic or less optimistic about Nvidia in a post-Jensen world, whenever that arrives? Another analogy that Jensen’s talked about, “It’s we, not I”, and that’s a very Apple-like thing too, famously not saying who did what. But the net result is that just meant Steve Jobs got credited for everything and there’s a bit now, “Well, Jensen Huang gets credited for everything”, but then you’re almost making the case, “Well actually, that’s probably deserved”. Then again, Apple, at least financially, has done very well in this post-Steve Jobs era, and yet when you are listing companies that Nvidia employees go to when they feel like they don’t fit in, you said Apple, and maybe they would’ve felt differently fifteen years ago. What’s your view going forward?

TK: Financially, I agree with you, but if you take a step back, what has Apple created in terms of innovation? They’re just so far behind in everything and they’re running on this platform that Steve Jobs laid the foundation and created, there isn’t really anything new. The Apple Car kind of fell apart, they’re nowhere in AI. So, yes, the Apple iPhone is this amazing platform that Tim Cook’s been able to shepherd and make hundreds of billions of dollars, etc., but in terms of actual technology innovations, I think it’s hard-pressed to say that Apple has really innovated.

But in a similar vein with Nvidia, if say Jensen disappears tomorrow and decides to retire, which is not going to happen because he loves Nvidia, but say that he does, I don’t know, Jensen is so ingrained. Part of why Nvidia is so able to do what it does is that he is so ingrained and has his finger on the pulse of everything that happens in the company…

He’s fashioned Nvidia. Nvidia, it’s like an exoskeleton for him.

TK: That exact analogy, he says he built Nvidia, where he’s like the race car driver of a Formula One car. He literally says that, like, “I built Nvidia in a way where I could drive it, and manage it, and steer it perfectly”. So, without Jensen there, do I see another CEO that’s reading 100 top-five emails a day, that is looking at all the AI discussion email lists inside a company, trading AI papers with his top engineers? I don’t know. I’ve met all the top Nvidia people, they’re all impressive, but they’re not on the Jensen level.

It goes back to the functional organization bit. You get a bunch of people who are absolute best in their field and so you, as the person in the center that is involved in everything, has awareness of everything, gets to direct the best possible resource at every sort of opportunity. But that, by definition, means there isn’t space in the organization for other generalists, right?

This was a thing at Apple, again just to go back to that analogy. And again, this was fifteen years ago, when Steve Jobs was still there so probably a bit of a different world. But there was a very sort of stern, “This is not the place for generalists”, like, “You come here to be a specialist, if you get a job here, you should expect you’ll never have a different job because we want you to be the best at what you do, we’re not interested in multiple experiences across business units and things along those lines”. But that works when it’s all flowing up to one node that is the ultimate generalist that has the view and understanding of everything and it’s incredibly effective. But yeah, it’s not good for succession planning, it makes it pretty tough.

And yet, despite Nvidia’s reliance on Huang, the board and the powers that be decided he had to go, in direct opposition to the preferences of Nvidia’s nominal owners, i.e. shareholders. And, like I said, I thought they had succeeded; tech may have made it increasingly possible for a dwindling number of employees to deliver outsized revenue and valuations, but ultimately any individual would be deemed expendable, particularly in the face of a coordinated media campaign and the opposition of the national security apparatus.

But I was wrong. And, ultimately, even if you think what happened this weekend was wrong — including President Trump calling into an Nvidia board meeting to press for Huang’s reinstatement — this moment does strike me as both unique in terms of the clear exception that Huang has obviously been deemed to be (and not without merit), and also a harbinger of the future. It only takes an individual.

The Bimodal Distribution

The world is, make no mistake, growing more complex. The tools we have to master that complexity, however, are not just improving, they actually thrive on complexity. When I’m trying to teach someone how to use AI, one of my first pieces of advice is to talk more (and yes, talking is better than typing); you can’t overwhelm the AI with information, it’s dealing in information at an unimaginable scale....

blogs.title: Amazon Earnings, The Chip Question, About Agents
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Amazon makes the case they are not like other compute providers, even as they signal the willingness to give up margin to serve the frontier.
blogs.content:
Amazon makes the case they are not like other compute providers, even as they signal the willingness to give up margin to serve the frontier.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

On last week’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I continue to discuss the Jensen Huang situation, why I think everyone is thinking about agentic commerce wrong, and why I love the iPhone Duo.

Then, on Sunday’s subscriber only mailbag , we discuss our decision to embrace video, whether disruption theory is still real, and the challenge of selling AI using worse AI.

This week is the Thanksgiving holiday; there will be an Update today and tomorrow only, and no Stratechery Interview. There will also be one Dithering episode on Tuesday, and a subscriber-only Sharp Tech on Wednesday.

On to the Update:

Amazon Earnings

It was, needless to say, a very busy November; so busy, in fact, that I am only just now getting to Amazon’s earnings, which dropped at the end of October. From Bloomberg :

Amazon.com Inc. shares dropped after the company reported greater capital spending than anticipated and the slowest growth in the core e-commerce business in three years. Amazon said it spent more than $77 billion on property and equipment in the third quarter, far more than analysts’ estimates, while pursuing its effort to build data centers and fulfill demand for artificial intelligence services. Third-quarter sales were lower than anticipated, rising 12% to $201.9 billion.

Revenue at the cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, accelerated for the sixth straight quarter. Online sales gained just 2% to $68.5 billion, the lowest increase since early 2023, when Amazon was still working through the post-pandemic slump in online retail. Advertising sales, a business closely tied to the e-commerce franchise, rose 11%, the slowest rate since Amazon began breaking out such results in 2020. The shares fell 4.4% to $233.10 as the markets opened in New York on Friday. The stock is up about 1% so far this year.

CEO Andy Jassy did not reassure investors on the earnings call about Amazon’s spending; in fact, he doubled down:

On the CapEx involved to grow the way we’re talking about, it’s meaningful. And I think that this — the way we think about it, Doug, is that this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. I think what we’re seeing with AI, it’s the biggest transformation in our lifetime. And if the idea of being able to grow 39% with $184 billion annual run rate and to grow 40% a year on top of that in each of the next 2 years and ultimately end up as $1 trillion-plus business, we’re going to invest to continue being the leader.

We are the leader today in the, I’ll call it, the infrastructure and AI space. And would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yes, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity. And we can fund this plan. And I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue. It will forever change our free cash flow. And we’re going to invest and we’re going to pursue it to continue to be the significant leader like we are today.

The part that I thought was notable — and very much in line with a lot of the analysis I’ve been doing on Stratechery this year — was Jassy’s implicit assumption that AI compute is on its way to being a commodity business; this was in response to a question about workloads running on Bedrock, AWS’s managed inference service:

Well, you’re right that the majority and most of Bedrock today is being run on top of Trainium. And we do that in meaningful part because we really like the price performance that we’re getting, and it allows us to both keep prices as low as possible for customers as well as we like the margins associated with it.

If you think about margins in the cloud space and you’re looking at different players and what their cost structure looks like, there are a few things to pay attention to. The first is for their data centers, how many of them are they actually buying or long leasing versus doing colo or neoclouds. I mean neoclouds are about 3,500 basis points worse in operating margin than if you long lease them. And then you look at what is the hardware on top of which they’re running, and if you’re using the hardware that everybody else is using, you’ll have a comparable cost structure to what everybody is doing. And if you have the ability to use hardware that’s different, you’ll have an advantage.

And so I think when you look at what we’re doing, most of our capacity is either owned or long leased which enjoys better operating margins than what you’ll find when people are mostly doing colo or neo or a big chunk doing colo or neo. And the fact that we’re running on top of our own chip that’s providing both advantaged price performance and it’s more cost effective for ourselves because we own it, I think, gives us some structural cost advantages that I think are going to be very helpful to customers as we pass them back to customers and helpful to the overall economics of AWS.

This is the bull case not for a time when compute is scarce, but for when compute is abundant, which, incidentally, is exactly what investors are freaking out about right now. In a commodity market price is not based on differentiation but rather marginal willingness to pay: how much is the last entity willing to pay for a unit of compute? And, if we were to enter a scenario where there simply aren’t enough entities for all of the compute that is available, then the price will fall to the marginal cost of the compute that clears the market; everyone whose marginal cost exceeds that will simply not sell. Everyone who can’t make enough operating profit to pay for their debt load will go bankrupt.

However, that doesn’t mean there won’t be real money to be made in such a market; profit will be a function of having a superior cost structure, which is exactly what Jassy is claiming AWS will have. Moreover, the entities with the superior cost structures will be the last to lose demand, precisely because they will have the most capacity to handle lower prices (indeed, they will attract it, because they will be safe to build on).

Meanwhile, Jassy continued to make the case — reasonably, I think — that inference benefits AWS broadly:

We have a compelling flywheel spinning in AWS. Borrowing from Jim Collins’ flywheel definition Good to Great, where if you do A, you almost can’t help but do B and if you do B, you almost can’t help but do C and so on. In AWS, having the leading functionality, security and operational performance can’t help but drive customers to run their apps and store their data in AWS, which can’t help but drive AWS AI demand because customers prefer their production inference to be near the rest of their data and apps, which can’t help but drive core AWS demand because AI uses core for work like reinforcement learning, posttraining and tool usage, which can’t help but drive reinvestment back into our broader AWS functionality.

This is a different model than primarily hosting GPUs or renting short-term data center capacity. This is a long-term platform strategy that broadly helps customers invent and evolve their customer experiences, operate stably and build a reliable partnership they can grow for many years. And it also yields very attractive long-term economics for us regardless of supply scarcity.

Or, per the point above, regardless of supply abundance! In short, Jassy’s overarching point seemed to be, “We are not the neoclouds”, and he’s right!

---

Presented by

One way to tell if something has become valuable is that people try to steal it. AI startups saw attempted transaction fraud rates up to 4.3x higher than other startups, according to Stripe .

Then companies got better at stopping it, so fraud moved upstream. Fraudulent actors started creating multiple accounts to claim free trials and tokens. That abuse rose 40% in six months.

Stripe Radar is adapting accordingly, using signals across the Stripe network to identify abuse at registration and login, before a payment ever happens. You can learn more at stripe.com/radar . 

---

The Chip Question

Jassy confirmed that Amazon will be selling Trainium chips:

Customers using our custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in Q3 alone, and we just open-sourced TorchNeuron so developers can run existing PyTorch code, which most already use on Trainium without rewriting a thing. As we launch new generations of chips, demand for prior generations remained strong. After our launch of Graviton5, backlog for prior generation Graviton instances still more than doubled quarter-over-quarter. And short-term capacity for prior generation Trainium instances sell at a premium compared to the first half of the year. With Trainium demand so strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027. Overall demand for AWS capacity remains exceptionally strong.

An analyst reasonably asked why, if inference demand is so strong, AWS wouldn’t just keep Trainium for itself; Jassy’s answer wasn’t very convincing:

On the balance of chips and what you sell externally versus what you use inside your cloud, it’s a very good question. And it’s a question that we’re continuing to evaluate as we speak. I would say that the number of companies who have a significant cloud business and a chip strong enough to sell externally is effectively two. So there really aren’t many customers that have to grapple with the same type of problem at this type of scale.

And at this point, everybody is producing their advanced chips with the same provider. There’s only so many chips that provider can provide each year. Everybody gets an allocation. And you have to decide with that allocation how much of it you want to sell externally and how much of it you want to use in your cloud. And there’s a trade-off. If you sell externally, you’re able to realize more revenue in the short term because you get to recognize the revenue as soon as it leaves your inventory. And on the flip side, if you decide to use it inside your cloud in the form of EC2 instances or Bedrock, you actually will end up driving more absolute revenue and free cash flow from those chips because you get to use them over 5 to 6 years and drive revenue for a longer period of time. So you have to really think through what you want to do.

To date, I would say that we’ve taken a different approach in how we’ve used our chips than the other provider who has the same type of balancing act going on. And as I mentioned earlier, we believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally, and we’re going to start in late 2027. And we will be thinking through that balance, I think, probably every year. But they’ll both be very significant. Our ability to create price performance, scalable chips is going to be a very significant strategic advantage for us at scale, both in our own cost structure as well as building a separate business and selling external chips and selling external chips really is a very different business than your cloud infrastructure business.

I admit, posting that entire answer was kind of a waste of time, but it’s always funny when executives clearly don’t want to answer a specific question. And some of the points were accurate! Only Amazon and Google make their own LLM accelerators at scale, and both are dependent on TSMC in the end, and have to make hard allocation decisions. And, critically, both have to make the same allocation decision, which, I strongly suspect, is “Do we want to keep Anthropic as a customer?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI are the two companies with sufficient demand to have leverage over Amazon (and Google), and, in the long run, they don’t want to pay Amazon and Google inference m...
